coredata.dc:description: A second gene (pueB, polyurethane esterase B) encoding an extracellular polyurethanase (PueB) was cloned from Pseudomonas chlororaphis into Escherichia coli. The recombinant polyurethanase showed esterase activity when assayed with various p-nitrophenyl substrates and lipase activity when assayed with triolein. Nucleotide sequencing of pueB showed an open reading frame of 1695 bp encoding a 60-kDa protein of 565 amino acid residues, with the serine hydrolase consensus sequence GXSXG and a C-terminal secretion signal (G-G-X-G-X-D-X-X-X). Unlike the PueA polyurethanase, PueB contains a putative N-terminal signal peptide. Comparison between the amino acid and nucleotide sequences of these two genes revealed that they share 42% and 59% identity respectfully. Parsimony analysis of the predicted amino acid sequences for the PueB, PueA, and other polyurethanase enzymes and similar lipase enzymes was performed. Interestingly the polyurethanase enzymes do not form a single cluster, but appear to be distributed among multiple lineages. These analyses suggest that the polyurethanase enzymes thus far studied have evolved from lipases, and are not derived from a single source.

head.ce:title: Cloning, nucleotide sequencing and characterization of a polyurethanase gene (pueB) from Pseudomonas chlororaphis

ce:affiliation.ce:textfn: Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, SLU 10736, Hammond, LA 70402, USA

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A second gene (pueB, polyurethane esterase B) encoding an extracellular polyurethanase (PueB) was cloned from Pseudomonas chlororaphis into Escherichia coli. The recombinant polyurethanase showed esterase activity when assayed with various p-nitrophenyl substrates and lipase activity when assayed with triolein. Nucleotide sequencing of pueB showed an open reading frame of 1695 bp encoding a 60-kDa protein of 565 amino acid residues, with the serine hydrolase consensus sequence GXSXG and a C-terminal secretion signal (G-G-X-G-X-D-X-X-X). Unlike the PueA polyurethanase, PueB contains a putative N-terminal signal peptide. Comparison between the amino acid and nucleotide sequences of these two genes revealed that they share 42% and 59% identity respectfully. Parsimony analysis of the predicted amino acid sequences for the PueB, PueA, and other polyurethanase enzymes and similar lipase enzymes was performed. Interestingly the polyurethanase enzymes do not form a single cluster, but appear to be distributed among multiple lineages. These analyses suggest that the polyurethanase enzymes thus far studied have evolved from lipases, and are not derived from a single source.

ce:section.ce:para: Polyurethanes (PUs) are a class of plastics that are widely used as raw materials in various industries. Polyurethanes are synthesized from polyols and polyisocyanates, and are classified into two types, polyester PUs and polyether PUs. Polyester PUs are considered to be comparatively susceptible to microbial degradation (Morton and Surman, 1994). Despite its xenobiotic origins, PU has been found to be susceptible to biodegradation by naturally occurring microorganisms (Pathirana and Seal, 1984; Bentham et al., 1987; Kay et al., 1991). Enzymatic attack on PUs could be contributed by hydrolases such as ureases attacking the urea bonds, proteases attacking the amide bonds, and esterases attacking the many ester bonds (Evans and Levisohn, 1968; Hole, 1972; Flip, 1978; and Griffin, 1980).

In a previous report from this lab (Howard et al., 1999) stationary growth of Pseudomonas chlororaphis utilizing PU as the sole carbon and energy source was observed within 9 h in batch culture. The generation time for this bacterium was calculated to be 45 min . When the bacterium was grown on PU agar plates, zones of clearing were observed within 18 h . The enzymes from P. chlororaphis responsible for polyurethane degradation were found to be extracellular. Zymogram analysis of the extracellular soluble proteins from P. chlororaphis using non-denaturing polyacrylamide gels revealed three PUase active protein bands with R f values of 0.25, 0.417, and 0.917. Upon purification of the three polyurethanase enzymes, these proteins were observed to have a molecular mass of 65, 60 and 31 kDa (Howard et al., 1999; Ruiz et al., 1999a, b).

Extracellular esterase activity is the primary activity found in both bacteria and fungi, which allow them to grow on PU. Six bacterial proteins (Howard and Blake, 1999; Howard et al., 1999; Allen et al., 1999; Ruiz et al., 1999b; Akutsu et al., 1998) and one fungal protein (Crabbe et al., 1994) have been purified and five of these enzymes, polyurethanases, demonstrate esterase activity with little or no proteolytic activity. Recently, three of the bacterial polyurethanases have been cloned and expressed in E. coli (Vega et al., 1999; Stern and Howard, 2000; Nomura et al., 1998). Two of these enzymes are either secreted from Pseudomonas fluorescens (Vega et al., 1999) or Pseudomonas chlororaphis (Stern and Howard, 2000), while the third is found in Comamonas acidovorans (Nomura et al., 1998) and is membrane-associated. In the present study, a gene (pueB) encoding a 60 kDa secreted polyurethanase from Pseudomonas chlororaphis has been cloned, sequenced and its encoded-protein characterized.

ECL nucleic acid labeling kit was obtained from Amersham (Arlington Heights, IL). Lambda Zap II and Gigapack III Gold packaging extract were obtained from Stratagene (La Jolla, CA). Enzyme substrates used were p-nitrophenyl acetate (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) and hide powder azure (Calbiochem, La Jolla, CA). The nylon membrane for blotting was S & S Nytran from Schleicher & Schuell (Keene, NH). Restriction enzymes and T4 DNA ligase were obtained from Sigma (St. Louis, MO) or GibcoBRL (Grand Island, NY). All other buffers and salts were reagent grade or better. Pseudomonas chlororaphis was isolated from a microbial consortium obtained from the Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC by using its ability to degrade water dispersible polyurethane, Impranil DLN. Pseudomonas chlororaphis was grown in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium at 30°C with constant shaking at 180 rpm . E. coli XL1-Blue MRF’ cells were obtained as part of the Lambda Zap II kit and were grown in LB medium at 37°C with shaking at 220 rpm .

Non-denaturing (ND) polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) was run with a 12% polyacrylamide resolving gel as described by Calza et al. (1985). Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-PAGE was performed as described by Laemmli (1970) with a 12% polyacrylamide resolving gel. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie blue staining.

During purification, aliquots of the protein fractions were spotted on YES agar plates supplemented with Impranil at pH 6.8 and examined for zones of clearing at 30°C. Assays to determine the proteolytic activity of the enzyme used hide powder azure in 50 mM phosphate buffer at pH 6.8 (Chavira et al., 1984). Activity against hide powder azure was determined by monitoring the increase in absorbance at 595 nm . One unit of activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that changes the absorbance at 595 nm by 0.01 min −1 . In addition, the enzyme was assayed for esterase activity by its ability to release ρ-nitrophenol from 8 mM ρ-nitrophenylacetate in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8 at 30°C (Deshpande et al., 1984). One unit of esterase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that produced 1 μmol of ρ-nitrophenol per min. All enzyme assays were observed to be linear with respect to time and protein concentration under the tested conditions.
Protein concentrations were estimated by the method of Kalb and Bernlohr (1977).

Chromosomal DNA was isolated by the method of Marmur (1961). The DNA was extracted two times with ether to remove trace organics (Sambrook et al., 1989). Lambda Zap II phage library was constructed as previously described (Vega et al., 1999). Recombinant phage were screened by plating in soft agar overlays containing Impranil as previously described (Vega et al., 1999). Plasmids containing pueB were excised and rescued from the λ library using the Stratagene protocol. The E. coli XL1-Blue were plated on LB agar plates supplemented with 1.5% (v/v) Impranil DLN Dispersion and 60 μgml −1 ampicillin. Plasmid DNA was isolated by the alkaline lysis method as described by Sambrook et al. (1989).

Chromosomal DNA from P. chlororaphis was digested to completion with EcoRI. The digested DNA fragments were fractionated along with an EcoRI digest of pPU13 by agarose gel electrophoresis (0.7% wtvol −1 ) using TAE buffer. The DNA fragments were transferred to a Nytran membrane by capillary action. The EcoRI fragment of the recombinant plasmid was excised from an agarose gel, purified by the Geneclean Kit (Bio 101, Inc., Gaithersburg, MD) and labeled using the ECL direct nucleic acid labeling and detection system (Amersham Life Sciences). Hybridizations were carried out overnight at 42°C as suggested by manufacture's specifications. Membranes were washed for 30 min with 0.1X SSC/0.1% SDS at 42°C prior to autoradiography.

Plasmids were excised and rescued from the λ library by co-infection of XL1-Blue cells with λPU13 and helper phage R408. The resulting plasmid containing PUase activity, pPU13, was isolated and subjected to restriction endonuclease digestion with EcoRI, KpnI, AccI, SalI, SmaI, ClaI, BglII, BamHI, NotI, HindIII, PvuI, XbaI, XhoI, and EcoRV (Bethesda Research Laboratories). Conditions used were those specified by the supplier. DNA fragments were fractionated by electrophoresis in TAE buffer with agarose gels, and sizes were estimated by comparison to a 1-kb DNA ladder.

The P. chlororaphis DNA fragment (3.2 kb) contained in the pApa3.2 recombinant plasmid was sequenced by automated microsequencing performed in the Sequencing Laboratory of the Biotechnology Center at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Both strands were sequenced and alignment was deduced using Sequencher 3.0. Homology searches were conducted against the GeneBank and EMBL data bases by using the BLAST program.
The nucleotide sequence of the 1800-bp DNA region containing the pueB gene has been deposited in the GeneBank database under accession no. AF188366.

The evolutionary history of the polyurethenases was inferred from the phylogenetic analysis of four PUases, five lipases, and an esterase outgroup. The predicted amino acid sequence was analyzed within a parsimony framework. Because the number of nucleotide changes required to cause a protein substitution is asymmetrical among codons, a step matrix was used to take these changes into account. The aligned amino acid sequences included inferred gaps and these gaps were treated as an additional character (a 21st amino acid) in the parsimony analysis. General descriptive statistics (CI, RI, RC; Kluge and Farris, 1969; Farris, 1989) for evaluating the fit of the data to the tree were calculated. Bootstrap values (Felsenstein, 1985) were employed (1000 iterations) to estimate strength of node support and the permutation tail probability (PTP, Faith and Cranston, 1991) was calculated (100 iterations) to examine the data for the hint of phylogenetic signal. All analyses were conducted with the software PAUP* (Swofford, 1998).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression and purification of the polyurethanase
ce:section.ce:para: The recombinant clone, pPU13, was subjected to Exonuclease III/Mung Bean Nuclease (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA) treatment to produce unidirectional deletions. This technique takes advantage of Exo III's requirement for double-stranded DNA; Exo III will not digest 3′ single strand overhangs, but will digest 3′ ends from blunt or 5′ overhangs. The polylinker in the pBluescript vector places unique 3′ restriction sites on the outside edge of the polylinker, and 5′ and blunt restriction sites internally. In order to create deletions in the insert but not the vector DNA, the clone is double digested with a 3′ (SacI) and 5′ (Bam HI) restriction enzyme and followed with ExoIII/Mung Bean Nuclease treatment. The deleted clones were ligated with T4 DNA ligase and transformed into E. coli XL1-Blue cells and screened for PUase activity on LB-polyurethane agar plates containing 100 μgml −1 ampicillin (Stern and Howard, 2000). A recombinant clone, pPU13Δ2.5, which 2.5 kb of the insert was deleted but still retained PUase activity was used for induction and purification. The recombinant (100 ml culture) was grown at 37°C to an OD600=0.6 in LB medium containing 60 μgml −1 ampicillin. At this time, isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG, 200 mgml −1 stock) was added to a final concentration of 1 mM . After 2 h the cells were harvested by centrifugation and resuspended in 7 ml of 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer pH 7.0. The cells were lysed by sonication and centrifuged (8000×g at 4°C) for 10 min in order to remove cell debris. The supernatant was fractionated by anion exchange using a DEAE-cellulose column (3×14 cm) with a bed volume of 53 ml . The column was equilbrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 6.8). A linear step-wise gradient of 0–1.0 MNaCl was applied. The enzyme activity was eluted in the 0.3 MNaCl fraction. One milliliter aliquots of the 0.3 MNaCl fraction were applied to a Sephadex G-75 column (45.0×1.0 cm) at a flow rate of 0.3 mlmin −1 and 1 ml fractions were collected. Polyurethanase activity was detected as a zone of clearing using a radial diffusion assay (RDA). The gel for the assay was made using 1.5% (w/v) agarose and 1.5% (v/v) Impranil DLN dispersion in 10 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.0. The wells held a maximum volume of 100 μl , and usually a zone of clearing would be evident in 6 h at 23°C, which was dependent on enzyme concentration.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Screening the λ library for pueB
ce:section.ce:para:
A genomic library was previously constructed (Stern and Howard, 2000) by ligating 4–10 kb
EcoRI fragments of P. chlororaphis chromosomal DNA into the EcoRI site of λZAPII. Screening for polyurethanase activity was based on the ability of the recombinants to hydrolyze polyurethane. The hydrolysis was evident as a readily distinguishable plaque, which was more translucent, than neighboring plaques since the milky-white polyurethane, Impranil, was hydrolyzed. Although plaques were evident after an overnight incubation at 37°C, the polyurethanase activity did not appear until the plates were transferred to 30°C for several hours. A total of 4000 recombinants were screened, and 20 polyurethanase-positive clones were isolated. However, from the restriction endonuclease patterns of the PUase positive clones in λZAPII, 11 isolates were identified as a single clone encoding PueA (Stern and Howard, 2000), three were identified as a single clone encoding PueB (this study), and six were unstable and lost.

Plasmid excision and rescue was carried out from one of the three unique clones encoding PueB and the resulting pBluescript plasmid (pPU13) was harbored in E. coli XL1-Blue. Restriction endonuclease mapping of pPU13 showed that the clone contained a recombinant insert of 5.7 kb (Fig. 1). To insure that the insert in pPU13 was from the P. chlororaphis chromosome, Southern blot hybridization was conducted. A chemi-luminescent probe was constructed from the 5.7 kb insert by labeling it with horseradish peroxidase. The probe hybridized strongly to the 5.7 kb insert and to the same-sized fragments from the chromosomal DNA indicating that the insert had originated from P. chlororaphis and that only one copy of the gene is present on the chromosome (Fig. 2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Nucleotide sequence of pueB and the translated ORF
ce:section.ce:para:
Upon sequencing the DNA insert of the 3.2 kb
ApaI fragment within pPU13, an open reading frame (ORF; pueB) was found in the pApa3.2 subclone by codon analysis, starting with an ATG codon in nucleotide 63 and stopping with a TGA codon in nucleotide 1758 (Fig. 3). The initiating ATG codon was preceded 7 nucleotides by a plausible ribosome binding site with an AGGA. The ORF of pueB encoded a polypeptide of 565 amino acids with a molecular mass of 59.8 kDa . The first 37 deduced amino acids showed the characteristics of an N-terminal signal secretion peptide. Two positively charged amino acids, lysine at positions 7 and 15, and two negative charged amino acids, aspartate at positions 6 and 13, were followed by an 11 amino acid hydrophobic core. A helix breaking proline residue, at position 33, was observed four amino acids before the putative cleavage site at Ala37.

Further analysis of the ORF showed two regions of special interest, one a putative active site and the other a region found to be conserved in secreted lipases that contain a C-terminal secretion signal. The serine hydrolase motif, G-X-S-X-G, was found at Gly148, while the secretion consensus signal was found at Gly328. The active site and secretion signal sequences align well with conserved regions within extracellular lipases found by using a BLASTP search of Genbank at the National Center for Biotechnology. All of the lipases compared contain a small but highly conserved region in the active site. In each of the proteins X 1 was conserved with a histidine and X 2 was conserved with a leucine. The serine hydrolase active site is consistent with the inhibition observed by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) on enzyme activity for PueB. A second conserved region was observed for PueB and the other lipases. A common motif among secreted lipases (Akatsuka et al., 1994; Doung et al., 1994) was observed at amino acids 307–343. The secretion sequence motif, G-G-X-G-X-D-X-X-X was conserved as well as its location. Interestingly, the location of the secretion motif is consistently 163 amino acid residues downstream from the putative catalytic motif for each of the polypeptides.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison of PueB with other lipases
ce:section.ce:para: A BLASTP search (Altschul et al., 1997) of Genebank using the amino acid sequence encoded by pueB, yielded seven protein sequences of significant identity five that are extracellular lipases and two that are extracellular polyurethanases (Table 1). PueB showed the greatest amino acid identity with the polyurethanase, PueA (42%), from Pseudomonas chlororaphis, the Lipase (39%) from Pseudomonas fluorescens MIS38 and LipA lipase (36%) from Serratia marcescens. The next greatest identities were with the LipApf33 (27%) from Pseudomonas fluorescens 33, TliA lipase (26%) from Pseudomonas fluorescens and the Lipase (25%) from Pseudomonas fluorescens SIK W1, and the polyurethanase, PulA (24%) from Pseudomonas fluorescens. PueB showed no significant identity with the PUase, PudA (11%), from Comamonas acidovorans. PudA possesses a high degree homology only with the catalytic region of the serine hydrolase family of proteins. The PudA polyurethanase was shown to be a membrane protein and the highest degree of homology was detected with the Torpedo californica acetylcholinesterase, T AchE (Normura et al., 1998).

In addition to the BLASTP analysis, parsimony analysis of the predicted amino acid sequences for the PueB, PueA, PudA and PulA polyurethanase enzymes and similar lipase enzymes was performed. The EstA, tributryin esterase, from Lactococcus lactis subspecis cremoris was chosen as the outgroup. A single most parsimonious tree at 3608 steps with descriptive statistics of CI=0.80, RI=0.67, RC=0.54 was recovered (Fig. 4). Of the 675 characters, 490 were parsimony informative. Character support for nodes ranged from 29 to 206. Based on the PTP (0.01), phylogenetic signal was present in the data, but the quality or quantity of that signal is uncertain (Slowinski and Crother, 1998). In broad terms, the phylogeny does not indicate monophyletic groupings (single origins) of the PUases or lipases. Bootstrap values range from weak to strong (50–100) but do support the polyphyletic origin of PUases.

The recombinant clone, pPU13Δ2.5, which 2.5 kb of the insert from pPU13 was deleted but still retained PUase activity, was used for induction and purification. The recombinant (100 ml culture) was grown at 37°C to an OD600=0.6 in LB medium containing 60 μgml −1 ampicillin. At this time, isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG, 200 mgml −1 stock) was added to a final concentration of 1 mM . After 2 h the cells were harvested by centrifugation and resuspended in 7 ml of 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer pH 7.0. The cells were lysed by sonication and centrifuged (8000×g at 4°C) for 10 min in order to remove cell debris. The supernatant was fractionated by anion exchange using a DEAE-cellulose column (3×14 cm ) with a bed volume of 53 ml . The column was equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 6.8). A linear step-wise gradient of 0–1.0 MNaCl was applied. The enzyme activity was eluted in the 0.3 MNaCl fraction. One milliliter aliquots of the 0.3 MNaCl fraction were applied to a Sephadex G-75 column (45.0×1.0 cm) at a flow rate of 0.3 mlmin −1 and 1-ml fractions were collected. The recombinant, cytoplasmic PUase protein, PueB, was purified to apparent electrophoretic homogeneity as indicated by the appearance of a single band on a SDS-PAGE gel (Fig. 5). A plot of log MW versus R f for the SDS-PAGE gel indicates a single 60 kDa protein.

Unlike the recombinant PueA polyurethanase, E. coli did not secrete the recombinant PueB polyurethanase. Phenotypic expression of the recombinant cells was not observed until 6–10 days incubation. The majority of the protein was localized in the cytoplasm of the E. coli cells. In addition, the PueB displayed an alpha-zone of clearing on polyurethane containing agar plates. The presence of an N-terminal signal peptide may contribute to the inability of E. coli to secrete this protein.

A radial diffusion assay using rhodamine B agar plates (Kouker and Jaeger, 1987) supplemented with either the polyester-polyurethane, ImpranilTM DLN, (Bayer Corp) or triolein (Sigma) as the substrate was incorporate to assay PueB for polyurethanase and lipase activities. Rhodamine B agar plates, 0.001% (wtvol −1), were prepared in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.0, containing either polyurethane, 3.0 gl −1 , or triolein, 0.1% (volvol −1) as a final concentration. When assaying for enzyme activity, wells of 1.0 cm diameter were cut and charged with the appropriate amount of purified enzyme. The plates were incubated at 30° C for 18–20 h . Agar plates containing substrate and rhodamine B appear opaque and are pink colored. Enzyme activity was monitored by irradiating plates with UV light at 350 nm . After 18 h of incubation, PUase and lipase activities could be detected as an orange fluorescence and with extended incubation fluorescent halos were formed around the wells (Fig. 6).

In addition to the PUase and lipase activities, catalytic properties of the purified PUase protein, PueB, revealed esterase activity. Using ρ-nitrophenylacetate as the esterase substrate, the purified protein displayed a specific activity of 9.8 Umg −1 . In addition, the enzyme exhibited activity against ρ-nitrophenylpropionate (6.2 Umg −1 ), ρ-nitrophenylbutyrate (11.9 Umg −1 ), ρ-nitrophenylcaproate (12.4 Umg −1 ), and ρ-nitrophenylcaprylate (13.5 Umg −1 ). The enzyme activity was stable after 10 min at 100°C, and the esterase activity was inhibited 50% by the addition of 1 mMPMSF .

The use of phage λ as a cloning vector in this study enabled the cloning of large fragments of P. chlororaphis DNA. The library in theory (average insert size approx. 7 kb ) was large enough to represent the entire chromosome several times, however the 31 kDa PUase purified previously (Ruiz et al., 1999b) was not obtained. The failure to isolate this PUase gene might be due to the restriction endonuclease EcoRI, used to generate the library, cleaving the gene such that phenotypic expression is not observed or the gene is contained on a larger (>10 kb ) EcoRI DNA fragment. Two genes encoding polyurethanases in P. chlororaphis have been cloned in E. coli. Both genes can be expressed in E. coli however, the PueA enzyme is secreted and displays a beta zone of clearing on polyurethane agar plates while PueB is not secreted and displays an alpha zone of clearing of polyurethane agar plates. Both enzymes confer esterase activity towards ρ-nitrophenyl substrates, are temperature stable up to 100 C and the esterase activity is inhibited by the addition of 1 mMPMSF .

In an earlier study (Howard et al., 1999), three polyurethanase enzymes were observed from P. chlororaphis. These PUases were found to be extracellular, displayed esterase activity against ρ-nitrophenylacetate and inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride. Upon cloning the 65 kDa , PueA, polyurethanase from P. chlororaphis in E. coli, the recombinant protein was secreted by the host, displayed a beta zone of clearing on polyurethane containing agar plates and was noted to have a high homology to Group I lipases (Stern and Howard, 2000). These types of lipases do not contain an N-terminal signal peptide but instead a C-terminal secretion signal. The secretion of these enzymes occurs in one step through a tree-component ATP-binding cassette transporter (Arpigny and Jaeger, 1999).

In a related study (Wales and Sagar, 1988), two types of polyurethanase activities were observed from Asperigillus terreus, which were attributed to endopolyurethane and exopolyurethane activity. The endopolyurethane activity resulted in a decrease in the degree of polymerization through the cleaving of bonds along the polymer chain. It was hypothesized that this enzyme affect accounted for the alpha zone of clearing where a weakly translucent zone was observed. Exopolyurethane activity, which is involved in the removal of successive monomer units from the ends of the polymer chains, could account for the visible clearing seen in the beta zone clearing.

In lipases and other serine hydrolyses, the active serine residue forms a catalytic triad in which an aspartate or glutamate and a histidine participate (Jaeger et al., 1994; Persson et al., 1989; Winkler et al., 1990). In true lipases, X1 is occupied mostly by histidine or tyrosine and X2 is variable. Sequence analysis of the two polyurethanase genes revealed that both genes contain a serine hydrolase active site (G-H-S-L-G) and a C-terminal secretion signal (G-G-X-G-X-D-X-X-X). Unlike the PueA polyurethanase, PueB contains a putative N-terminal signal peptide. Comparison between the amino acid and nucleotide sequences of these two genes revealed that they share 42% and 59% identity, respectively. Parsimony analysis of the predicted amino acid sequences for the PueB, PueA, and PulA polyurethanase enzymes and similar lipase enzymes was also performed. Interestingly the polyurethanase enzymes do not form a single cluster, but appear to be distributed among multiple lineages. These analyses suggest that the polyurethanase enzymes thus far studied have evolved from lipases, and are not derived from a single source.

From the BLASTP search of Genebank, the seven proteins with the greatest amino acid identity with PueB have been classified as Group I lipases (Arpigny and Jaeger, 1999; Ruiz and Howard, 1999; Stern and Howard, 2000). The characteristics of Group I lipases are molecular weights ranging from 45 to 65 kDa , 51–80% identity, a serine hydrolase active site (G-X-S-X-G), the absence of an N-terminal signal peptide, and a C-terminal secretion signal sequence. While the five related lipases varied in total amino acid residues the active site and the secretion signal sequences aligned perfectly indicating these are well-conserved enzymes. Although PueB contains a serine hydrolase active site (G-X-S-X-G), a C-terminal secretion signal sequence, and a comparable molecular weight (59.8 kDa ), this protein appears to contain an N-terminal signal peptide and a lower percent identity with the Group I lipases.

Studies are under way to define the structure of these PUase enzymes and role that they have in polyurethane degradation by more detailed analysis of deletions and mutations. The results obtained from these studies will contribute to the understanding of the activity and structure–function relationships of the PUase enzymes, of the regulation of the genes for these enzymes, and the metabolic pathway(s) of polyurethane degradation. Future comparisons between the biochemical properties of the two corresponding enzymes, PueA and PueB, should be very informative in regards to their roles as endo- and exo-polyurethanses in the degradation of polyurethane. This knowledge will provide a starting point for the eventual enhancement and bioremediation of polyurethane waste.
